71.title: The road to Emmaus (Luke 24:13–35)
71.hook: two sad travelers walk seven miles with a stranger and know him when he breaks bread
71.howItsDone: Many churches read the road to Emmaus in the Easter season, and some hold Emmaus walks on Easter Monday. Christians often speak of meeting Christ in scripture and in the breaking of bread, the two halves of many Sunday services.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mary Magdalene in the garden, and your line: he said her name. Whose name did you say kindly? Today a new stretch begins: the story keeps going. Day seventy-one.

After bad news, the walk home goes over it and over it. What happened. What should have happened. What it all means now. The same Sunday, Luke says, two followers of Jesus are walking away from Jerusalem, toward a village called Emmaus, threescore furlongs off, about seven miles. One is named Cleopas; the other, Luke never names. They're talking about everything that's happened: the arrest, the cross, and now a strange report from some women about an empty tomb. And a stranger falls into step beside them. Today, the road to Emmaus.
screen: `THE WALK HOME AFTER BAD NEWS.` → `SEVEN MILES TO EMMAUS.` → `A STRANGER FALLS INTO STEP.`

segments.voice: Luke tells us who it is, in the King James Bible: "Jesus himself drew near, and went with them. But their eyes were holden that they should not know him." He asks what they're talking about, and they stop, their faces sad. Cleopas says: are you the only visitor in Jerusalem who doesn't know? And then this line: "But we trusted that it had been he which should have redeemed Israel." We had hoped. Past tense. The stranger doesn't correct them right away. He walks with them, and, starting with Moses and all the prophets, explains the scriptures about the Messiah. Seven miles of conversation. When they reach the village, he acts as if he's going further, and they stop him: "Abide with us: for it is toward evening, and the day is far spent." The hymn Abide with Me borrows that line. At the table he takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and gives it to them. The same four movements as the last supper, and the feeding on the hillside. "And their eyes were opened, and they knew him; and he vanished out of their sight." And they say to each other: "Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?" They get up that same hour and walk the whole way back, though the day was far spent, to tell the others how he was known to them in the breaking of bread. Luke's story goes on in a second book, the Acts of the Apostles, and this road is the hinge between them. The story doesn't end at the tomb. It turns around on a road and keeps going.
screen: `THEIR EYES WERE HOLDEN.` · `WE HAD HOPED.` · `ABIDE WITH US.` · `KNOWN IN THE BREAKING OF BREAD.` · then, large: `DID NOT OUR HEART BURN WITHIN US?`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind one we had hoped of your own. A plan that fell through. A door that stayed shut. Someone who left. Say it the way the two did: I had hoped. Then let your mind walk back over the last few days, slowly, the way they looked back over the road. Was there a moment that warmed you while it was happening, a talk, a meal, a kindness, that you only noticed afterward? Rest there. If you pray, you can give thanks for it. The bell holds the time.
The road to Emmaus. Two sad travelers, a stranger who walks with them, and bread broken at a table, where they finally know him.
Your line: our hearts burned. Tonight, look back over the day for one moment that warmed you, and name it. Day seventy-one.

72.title: Thomas (John 20:24–29)
72.hook: the one who wanted proof gets invited to touch the wounds
72.carry: doubt is allowed in the room
72.howItsDone: Many churches read the story of Thomas on the Sunday after Easter, which Orthodox Christians call Thomas Sunday. The Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala, in India, trace their church to the apostle, and many churches keep his feast in July or December.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the road to Emmaus, and bread broken at evening. Your line was our hearts burned. Who did you walk with? Today, someone who wasn't there, and wasn't convinced. Day seventy-two.

You've missed something big. The group chat is exploding. Everybody was there except you, and now they're all telling you what happened, and it sounds impossible. Back in Jerusalem, there's a locked room. On the evening of that first Sunday, John says, Jesus came and stood among the disciples and said, peace be unto you, and showed them his hands and his side. But one of the twelve wasn't there. His name is Thomas, called Didymus, the twin. When the others tell him, we've seen the Lord, he doesn't just nod along. Today's word: Thomas.
screen: `EVERYONE WAS THERE BUT YOU.` → `A LOCKED ROOM, A FIRST SUNDAY.` → `THOMAS WASN'T THERE.`

segments.voice: Thomas says, in the King James Bible: "Except I shall see in his hands the print of the nails, and put my finger into the print of the nails, and thrust my hand into his side, I will not believe." That's where the phrase doubting Thomas comes from. But look at who he was before this. When Jesus decided to go back into Judea, where, his disciples reminded him, people had just tried to stone him, it was Thomas who said: "Let us also go, that we may die with him." And at the last supper, when Jesus spoke about going away, Thomas was the one honest enough to say, we don't know where you're going; how can we know the way? Read that way, Thomas doesn't look like a skeptic by nature. He's brave, and he asks the question others may be thinking. Eight days later, John says, the disciples are together again, and this time Thomas is with them. The doors are shut. Jesus stands among them: "Peace be unto you." And he goes straight to Thomas, and offers him exactly what he asked for: "Reach hither thy finger, and behold my hands; and reach hither thy hand, and thrust it into my side: and be not faithless, but believing." He doesn't throw Thomas out for doubting. He comes back for him. And here's a surprise: the text never says Thomas actually touched him. It just gives his answer: "My Lord and my God." Some readers hear it as one of the fullest confessions of who Jesus is in the Gospels, and it comes from the one who doubted. Then Jesus says: "blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed." Tradition says Thomas later carried the news as far as India, and the Saint Thomas Christians of Kerala trace their church to him.
screen: `EXCEPT I SHALL SEE.` · `LET US ALSO GO, THAT WE MAY DIE.` · `REACH HITHER THY FINGER.` · `THE DOUBTER'S CONFESSION.` · then, large: `MY LORD AND MY GOD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself get quiet. Think of one doubt you carry. About God, about faith, about something you were taught, or about yourself. Doubts are easy to keep hidden, as if having one means not belonging. Now say it out loud, gently. One sentence. Not as an attack, just as the truth. Notice what happens. In this story, Jesus didn't send Thomas out of the room; he came back for him. If you pray, you can bring the doubt to God just as it is. The bell holds the time.
Thomas. Called Didymus, the twin. The one who wanted proof, and who then said: my Lord and my God.
Your line: doubt is allowed in the room. Today, if someone near you shares a doubt, don't rush to fix it. Stay in the room with them. Day seventy-two.

73.title: Breakfast on the beach (John 21:1–19)
73.hook: by a charcoal fire, Jesus asks Peter three times: do you love me?
73.howItsDone: Many Christians read John 21 as the story of Peter's restoration after his denials, and preachers often use it to speak about forgiveness and second chances. Catholics and Orthodox Christians also read 'feed my sheep' as part of Peter's commission to lead.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Thomas: the one who wanted proof, invited to touch the wounds. Your line was doubt is allowed in the room. Did you stay in the room with someone's doubt? Day seventy-three.

Some things between friends never get mentioned. They just sit there, at every meal, in every silence. By the sea of Tiberias, in Galilee, some days after the empty tomb. Peter says he's going fishing, and six of the others go with him. All night, nothing. At dawn a figure on the beach calls out: throw the net on the right side of the boat. They do, and it fills so heavily they can't haul it in. One of them says, it is the Lord. Peter pulls on his coat and jumps into the water. On the shore a fire is already burning, with fish laid on it, and bread. And the figure says, come and have breakfast. But something is still sitting between Peter and Jesus. And the fire on that beach is the kind Peter has seen before.
screen: `ALL NIGHT, NOTHING.` → `IT IS THE LORD.` → `COME AND HAVE BREAKFAST.`

segments.voice: John uses one particular Greek word for a charcoal fire at two moments. The first is the night of the arrest, in the high priest's courtyard, where Peter stands warming his hands and says three times that he doesn't know Jesus. The second is here, on this beach. The same kind of fire. The same smell of smoke. After they eat, Jesus turns to Peter and asks, in the King James Bible: "Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?" Yes, Lord, Peter says, you know I love you. Feed my lambs. Then he asks again. And a third time. Three questions. Readers can hardly miss the match with three denials. And John says Peter was grieved that he asked a third time. Then Peter answers like someone with nothing left to prove: "Lord, thou knowest all things; thou knowest that I love thee." And Jesus says, "Feed my sheep." Notice what doesn't happen. Nobody brings up the courtyard. No lecture, no probation. Each yes is answered with a job: look after the people I love. Readers have long noticed that John's Greek uses two different verbs for love in this conversation, agapao and phileo, and they argue about whether it matters. Some hear a shift from one kind of love to another; others think John simply varies his words, the way he does elsewhere. The text doesn't settle it. Churches hear the charge differently too: Catholics and Orthodox Christians hear feed my sheep as Peter being given a shepherd's work in the church, and many Protestants hear it above all as a picture of what grace does for anyone who has failed. What they share is the shape: three denials, three loves, and then a future.
screen: `A CHARCOAL FIRE, TWICE.` · `LOVEST THOU ME? THREE TIMES.` · `EVERY YES GETS A JOB.` · `TWO GREEK WORDS FOR LOVE.` · then, large: `FEED MY SHEEP.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: offer someone a fresh start. Sit, and breathe slowly. Bring to mind someone who let you down. Not the worst thing, something ordinary. Picture them at breakfast with you, a fire going, the thing not yet mentioned. You don't have to pretend it didn't happen. Just picture handing them something to do again, a little trust back. If you pray, you can bring their name to God. If you don't, just hold the picture and notice how it sits in you. The bell holds the time.
Breakfast on the beach. A charcoal fire, fish and bread, and three questions that answer three denials.
Your line: three denials, three loves. Today, give someone a small fresh start: a message, a job, a door left open. Tomorrow, he's lifted out of sight. Day seventy-three.

74.title: The ascension (Acts 1:6–11)
74.hook: he's lifted out of sight, and two men ask why they're staring at the sky
74.howItsDone: Many churches celebrate Ascension Day on the Thursday forty days after Easter, and Christians confess in the Apostles' and Nicene Creeds that Jesus ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father.

segments.voice: Yesterday, breakfast on the beach: a charcoal fire and three questions. Your line was three denials, three loves. Who got a fresh start from you? Day seventy-four.

A car pulls away from the curb. A hand waves from the back window until the corner, and then the street is empty, and the person on the sidewalk keeps looking at the corner anyway. The Mount of Olives, just outside Jerusalem. Acts says that after the empty tomb Jesus kept appearing to his friends for forty days. Gathered with him one last time, they ask the question they've been carrying all along: is this the moment you restore the kingdom to Israel? He says the timing isn't theirs to know. Then, as they watch, he's lifted up, and a cloud takes him out of their sight. And they stand there. Staring at the sky.
screen: `WAVING FROM THE BACK WINDOW.` → `FORTY DAYS.` → `A CLOUD TAKES HIM.`

segments.voice: Just before he goes, Jesus gives them a map, and it turns out to be the map of the whole book of Acts: "ye shall be witnesses unto me both in Jerusalem, and in all Judaea, and in Samaria, and unto the uttermost part of the earth." Jerusalem first, then the countryside of Judea, then Samaria, the neighbors with an old quarrel, then everywhere. That's the order the story will travel. Then he's gone, and they're still looking up, and suddenly two men in white are standing beside them. In the King James Bible: "Ye men of Galilee, why stand ye gazing up into heaven?" It's almost funny. The sky has just opened, and the first thing heaven says is, why are you still standing here? The men promise he'll come back the same way he went. And then the disciples walk back down the hill to Jerusalem to wait, and to pray. Luke tells this scene twice, at the end of his Gospel and again at the start of Acts. Nothing in the text suggests a trip into outer space. In the Bible a cloud is an old sign of God's presence, from the cloud over Sinai to the bright cloud on the mountain of light, and the churches say, in the words of the old creeds, that he ascended into heaven and is seated at the right hand of the Father: Jesus taken fully into God's presence, and not gone for good. Christians differ on how literally to picture the rising itself, and the text doesn't explain how it looked. Many churches keep Ascension Day forty days after Easter, which puts it on a Thursday, though some move it to the Sunday after. But the heart of the story is the question. Stop staring. Go.
screen: `JERUSALEM, THEN THE ENDS OF THE EARTH.` · `WHY STAND YE GAZING?` · `A CLOUD MEANS GOD IS NEAR.` · `FORTY DAYS AFTER EASTER.` · then, large: `STOP STARING. GO.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: look up, then look around. If you can, go to a window or step outside. For the first part, just look up. Sky, ceiling, clouds, whatever's there. Let it be big. If you pray, you can let that be your prayer, without words. Then bring your eyes down, slowly, and look around at what's right in front of you: a street, a room, a person, a sink full of dishes. That's the kind of place the disciples were sent back to. Notice one thing there that needs you. The bell holds the time.
The ascension. Jesus taken up out of sight, forty days after Easter, and his friends sent back down the hill.
Your line: stop staring. go. Today, when you catch yourself waiting for a sign, do the next small thing in front of you instead. Tomorrow, wind and fire. Day seventy-four.

75.title: Pentecost (Acts 2:1–13)
75.hook: wind, flames, and every visitor hears the good news in their own language
75.howItsDone: Christians celebrate Pentecost fifty days after Easter as the coming of the Holy Spirit and the birthday of the church. Many churches decorate in red, read Acts 2, and sometimes read it aloud in several languages at once.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the ascension, and two men in white asking why everyone was staring at the sky. Your line was stop staring. go. What small thing did you do instead of waiting? Day seventy-five.

Think of a street market in a big city on a holiday weekend. Every stall shouting, every hotel full, a grandmother bargaining in one language while a kid answers her in another. That's Jerusalem on the morning of this story. It's a Jewish festival, the Feast of Weeks, and pilgrims have come from all over the known world. Acts lists them: Parthians and Medes, people from Mesopotamia, Egypt and Libya, Cretes, Arabians and visitors from Rome. Meanwhile, about a hundred and twenty followers of Jesus are together in one house, waiting, the way they were told to. And then, Acts says, there's a noise from the sky like a violent wind, and it fills the whole house. Out in the street, people hear it. A crowd comes running. And what they hear next makes no sense at all.
screen: `A CITY OF LANGUAGES.` → `ONE HOUSE, WAITING.` → `A SOUND LIKE WIND.`

segments.voice: Here it is in the King James Bible: "And there appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them." Flames, resting on each person. And they begin to speak in other languages. The crowd from all those countries hears Galileans, country people from up north, speaking their own mother tongues. They're stunned: "And how hear we every man in our own tongue, wherein we were born?" Some are amazed. Some sneer that they're full of new wine. And Peter stands up and says, they're not drunk, it's nine in the morning. The name Pentecost is Greek for the fiftieth day. Jews had long counted fifty days from Passover to the Feast of Weeks, Shavuot, a harvest festival that many Jews also came to link with the giving of the law at Sinai. That's why the city was full. Now look at what the miracle is, and what it isn't. Nobody is made to speak one language. Everyone hears in their own. The good news doesn't ask the crowd to cross over to it; it crosses over to them. Many Christians read this as the undoing of Babel, the old story where one language was scattered into many. Here the many languages stay, and understanding comes anyway. Christians call Pentecost the birthday of the church and keep it fifty days after Easter, often in red, the color of flame. They understand it as the coming of the Holy Spirit. Pentecostal churches take their name from this day, and many of them pray in tongues, while other churches understand the gift as belonging mainly to the early church, or as rare. What all of them keep is the picture: every language.
screen: `TONGUES LIKE AS OF FIRE.` · `EACH HEARS HIS OWN TONGUE.` · `PENTECOST: THE FIFTIETH DAY.` · `THE NEWS CROSSES OVER.` · then, large: `EVERY LANGUAGE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: greet someone in their language. Sit and breathe for a moment. Think of someone you'll see this week whose first language isn't yours, or whose language is a different kind: a grandparent's slang, a teenager's, a coworker's jargon. How would they say hello? If you know the words, say them quietly now, a few times, until they feel less strange in your mouth. If you don't, make a note to ask. If you pray, you can hold that person before God, in whatever language comes. The bell holds the time.
Pentecost. Greek for the fiftieth day: the Jewish Feast of Weeks, and for Christians the day the Spirit came, in flame and in every tongue.
Your line: every language. Today, greet one person in their language, even just one word. Tomorrow, the first community shares what it owns. Day seventy-five.

76.title: They shared everything (Acts 2:37–47)
76.hook: the first community breaks bread in homes and shares what they own
76.tomorrow: the beggar at the Beautiful Gate
76.howItsDone: Many churches hold up Acts 2:42 as a pattern for church life: teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer. Monastic communities and some Protestant communities hold property in common; many other Christians practice it through giving and shared meals.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pentecost: wind, flame, and a crowd from everywhere hearing their own mother tongues. Your line was every language. Whose language did you greet someone in? Day seventy-six.

A shared house has a group chat, and the group chat has opinions. Whose turn is it. Who ate the last of the bread. Sharing sounds lovely until it's Tuesday. Now go back to Pentecost, the same day. Peter has just finished speaking to the crowd, and Acts says they were cut to the heart, and asked: what shall we do? He tells them to turn around and be baptized, and about three thousand people do, in a single day. Three thousand new people, many of them visitors far from home, and a small group from Galilee who have no buildings, no budget and no plan. What happens next, Luke tells in one short paragraph.
screen: `WHAT SHALL WE DO?` → `THREE THOUSAND IN A DAY.` → `NO BUILDING, NO PLAN.`

segments.voice: Luke gives four things they kept doing: "And they continued stedfastly in the apostles' doctrine and fellowship, and in breaking of bread, and in prayers." Teaching, fellowship, bread, prayer. The word for fellowship is koinonia, from koinos, common, shared. It means having a share in something together, and Luke shows exactly what that looked like: "And all that believed were together, and had all things common." They sold property and possessions and gave to anyone as they had need. They met in the temple courts, and they broke bread in their homes, and here's the phrase our line comes from: they "did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart." Meat, in the King James Bible's English, just means food. Singleness of heart means a heart that isn't divided. Glad and simple hearts. Now the honest part. Acts doesn't pretend it stayed easy. A few chapters later there's a couple who lie about what they gave, and an argument about widows being left out of the daily food. And Christians have read this paragraph in different ways ever since. Monks and nuns took it as a pattern and hold everything in common to this day, as do some Protestant communities like the Hutterites. Many other Christians read it as a picture of radical generosity, given freely, rather than a rule for every church. What stands out, whichever way you read it, is that nobody is told to share. They just do. And the bread keeps turning up: in homes, around tables, day after day.
screen: `TEACHING, FELLOWSHIP, BREAD, PRAYER.` · `KOINONIA: HAVING A SHARE.` · `ALL THINGS COMMON.` · `IT DIDN'T STAY EASY.` · then, large: `GLADNESS AND SINGLENESS OF HEART.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: share one thing you own. Sit, and breathe. Let your mind walk through where you live, room by room. The shelf, the closet, the drawer, the kitchen. Look for one thing you have more of than you need, or something you love that someone else would love too. A book, a coat, a tool, a meal's worth of food. Don't decide how much. Just find one thing, and one person, or one place, it could go to. If you pray, you can offer it to God first. The bell holds the time.
They shared everything. The first community, three thousand new members in a day, breaking bread in their homes and holding what they had in common.
Your line: glad and simple hearts. Today, give away the one thing you found, and notice whether it makes you glad. Tomorrow, a man at a gate asks for money and gets something else. Day seventy-six.

77.title: The beggar at the Beautiful Gate (Acts 3:1–10)
77.word: The beggar at the Beautiful Gate
77.hook: Peter has no money, so he gives what he has: the man walks, leaps, praises
77.carry: such as I have, give I thee
77.howItsDone: Christians often quote Peter's words 'silver and gold have I none' when speaking about giving time, attention and care, and some churches' Sunday readings come from Acts 3 in the weeks after Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, they shared everything, breaking bread in their homes. Your line was glad and simple hearts. What did you give away? Eleven weeks on the path now. Day seventy-seven.

You're coming out of a store and someone by the door asks for change. You pat your pockets. Nothing. Who carries cash these days? So you do the little shrug, and the half smile, and you keep walking, and you don't quite look at them. Now go to the temple in Jerusalem, three in the afternoon, the hour of prayer. Peter and John are walking up. At one of the gates, the one called Beautiful, a man is lying on the ground. He's been unable to walk since birth. Every day, someone carries him here and puts him down by the gate, so he can ask the people going in to pray for a coin. He sees Peter and John, and he asks. And Peter has no money either.
screen: `NO CASH. THE SHRUG.` → `THE GATE CALLED BEAUTIFUL.` → `CARRIED THERE EVERY DAY.`

segments.voice: The first thing Peter does is stop. He fixes his eyes on the man, and says: look at us. Before anything else, the man is seen. He looks up, expecting a coin. And Peter says, in the King James Bible: "Silver and gold have I none; but such as I have give I thee: In the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth rise up and walk." Then he takes him by the right hand and lifts him up, and his feet and ankles grow strong. And Luke doesn't let him just stand there: "And he leaping up stood, and walked, and entered with them into the temple, walking, and leaping, and praising God." Walking and leaping. The man who was carried to the door every day goes in through it on his own feet. Notice the order. Peter doesn't pretend to have what he hasn't got. He doesn't feel bad about the empty pockets and walk on. He gives what he actually has. In the name of Jesus, for Christians, means by his authority and his power, not Peter's: the story is careful that Peter isn't the healer. And the people who see it know this man; they've walked past him for years. Where exactly was the Beautiful Gate? Nobody knows for certain. It's named nowhere else in the Bible, and scholars still debate which of the temple's gates it was. But the line has lasted: silver and gold have I none. Such as I have, give I thee.
screen: `LOOK ON US: FIRST, HE'S SEEN.` · `SILVER AND GOLD HAVE I NONE.` · `WALKING, AND LEAPING, AND PRAISING.` · `GIVE WHAT YOU ACTUALLY HAVE.` · then, large: `SUCH AS I HAVE GIVE I THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give what you actually have. Sit, and breathe. Ask yourself, honestly, what you have today. Maybe not money. Maybe not energy. But perhaps ten minutes. A skill. A kind word. A good ear. The ability to look someone in the eye and say, I see you. Pick one thing from that list, and one person who could use it. If you pray, you can offer it to God. If you don't, just hold it ready. The bell holds the time.
The beggar at the Beautiful Gate. Carried to the door for years, and now walking and leaping through it. This week: Emmaus, Thomas, a beach, a cloud, Pentecost, a shared table, and a gate.
screen: `THE BEGGAR AT THE BEAUTIFUL GATE — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: such as I have, give I thee. Today, when you can't give what's asked, give what you have, starting with a look. Tomorrow, a man who forgives as the stones fall. Day seventy-seven.
